value.overview: The Wrenthrush (Zeledonia coronata), also called Zeledonia, is a distinctive small songbird of the high mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is the only species in its genus and family. Despite its common name, it is not a true wren or thrush. The species lives mainly in cool, wet cloud forests and elfin forests, where it moves through dense vegetation searching for small invertebrates.
value.classification: The Wrenthrush belongs to the order Passeriformes and the family Zeledoniidae. It is the sole living species in the genus Zeledonia.
value.identification: The Wrenthrush has a compact, rounded body, a very short tail, short rounded wings, and a short, slightly pointed bill. Adults are mainly dark olive and gray, with a conspicuous yellow-orange crown patch bordered by black. The face, throat, breast, and belly are grayish, while the back and wings have an olive-bronze tone. Juveniles are browner and lack the clearly developed orange crown patch.
value.rangeHabitat: The Wrenthrush is restricted to the Talamancan highlands, occurring from northern and central Costa Rica southward through the Costa Rican mountains to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a high-elevation resident, especially associated with the Cordillera de Guanacaste, Cordillera Volcánica Central, Cordillera de Talamanca, and other cloud-forest ranges. It inhabits montane evergreen and elfin forests, usually in dense, wet vegetation near streams, mossy banks, bamboo, vines, and epiphytes, generally from about 1,500 to 3,500 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and essentially sedentary. In Costa Rica, it remains year-round in suitable highland forest and makes little regular seasonal or long-distance movement, although limited local elevational movement may occur.
value.breeding: Breeding has been recorded mainly from March through early July. The nest is a domed structure with a side entrance, built from moss, twigs, leaves, grass, and other plant material. Known nests have been placed in cavities or recesses in earthen banks and partly concealed by vegetation. Clutches recorded in a small number of nests contained three eggs. Both adults feed the nestlings, but incubation details remain poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Wrenthrush feeds primarily on arthropods, including spiders, caterpillars, and other insect larvae. It forages deliberately by hopping through dense undergrowth, moss, bamboo, vines, and epiphytes, examining leaves, branches, and the ground. Although it usually stays close to the forest floor, it may search several meters above the ground. Its short wings and rounded body suit maneuvering through tangled vegetation rather than sustained flight.
value.behavior: This species is secretive and often difficult to see, despite sometimes calling repeatedly. It usually moves by hopping through dense vegetation and is a weak flier that generally travels only short distances by air. Both sexes sing, and pairs may sing in duet. Vocal activity is especially noticeable during the breeding season, with singing often strongest around dawn and dusk, though calls can be heard throughout the day.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not well quantified but is considered broadly stable.
